content.title: Lucerne Festival: Away with Convention! Or Maybe Not?
content.lead: The Berlin Philharmonic, the New York Met Orchestra, and pianist of the century Martha Argerich: The Lucerne Festival hosts a summit of artists. Only some programs don't quite keep up.

image.author: Priska Ketterer / Lucerne Festival
image.caption: Martha Argerich as soloist in Beethoven's 2nd Piano Concerto with the Munich Philharmonic Orchestra under the direction of Lahav Shani.
image.altText: Lucerne Festival Summer 2026: Munich Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Lahav Shani with Martha Argerich as soloist. Lucerne, August 31, 2026. Copyright: Lucerne Festival / Priska Ketterer

content.caption: Martha Argerich as soloist in Beethoven's 2nd Piano Concerto with the Munich Philharmonic Orchestra under the direction of Lahav Shani.
content.author: Priska Ketterer / Lucerne Festival

content.text: How was it again? Festivals, organizers like to say, should offer the extraordinary: events, programs, works that one can only get from them, under the unique conditions of a festival – but by no means in the repertoire operations that provide basic cultural programming the rest of the year. That was once the theory, and it has worked for an astonishingly long time in classical music: Salzburg, Bayreuth, Aix, and Lucerne, together with a few other venues, set the standards; they crowned careers, set trends and fashions. But this monopoly has been increasingly shaky for about a decade.

In the battle for an audience that no longer comes as a matter of course but must be won over for each individual project, some concert and opera houses are now developing programs that make many festival programs seem stale. Routines are broken, forgotten works are unearthed, or new ones are commissioned, and many venues are increasingly succeeding in attracting younger audiences with unconventional formats. But what happens when a top ensemble ignores all efforts and offers a program that sounds like the past in every respect?

This was evident at the Berlin Philharmonic's most recent guest performance at the Lucerne Festival. Combining Tchaikovsky's 4th Symphony with Edward Elgar's «Enigma Variations» is neither risky nor particularly original; one can hear such things in regular symphony concerts, for example, at the Tonhalle. Moreover, it bore no connection to the main theme of the Lucerne Festival, which this summer aims to evoke a better America. So what did the German showcase ensemble and its chief conductor Kirill Petrenko intend with this?

Perhaps it was intended as a show of force: that an orchestra of this caliber is still able to set standards even with standard works and therefore deliberately refrains from experiments – precisely because it can. If that were the intention, it would at least be a statement, albeit a rather elitist one. The second guest concert by the Berliners at the KKL was certainly more appealing, as it featured a charming tension between the familiar and the unknown, which also drew the orchestra much further out of its much-invoked comfort zone.

image.author: Chris Christodoulou
image.caption: Kirill Petrenko has been chief conductor and artistic director of the Berlin Philharmonic since 2019.

content.caption: Kirill Petrenko has been chief conductor and artistic director of the Berlin Philharmonic since 2019.
content.author: Chris Christodoulou

content.text: For, in addition to Beethoven's Violin Concerto, which is always a special live event – especially thanks to the sensitive soloist Augustin Hadelich – Petrenko and his ensemble venture into Alexander Scriabin's 3rd Symphony. The work, subtitled «Le Divin Poème,» is rarely performed; it was even the Lucerne premiere of this typical turn-of-the-century piece. In it, music is not only intoxicatingly played but also intoxicatingly philosophized. In the spirit of Nietzsche, it is about the self-actualization of the ego, which, after all sorts of inner struggles, overcomes all metaphysics and, liberated, declares itself the «God» of its own existence. Utter nonsense, but fascinating, incredibly colorful music that does not deserve its shadowy existence.

Petrenko, the meticulous artist of sound and detail among conductors, lets the music seemingly speak entirely for itself – a clever strategy, because such ecstasies do not require additional outward expressions from the conductor's podium. With a similarly controlled approach, Riccardo Chailly had already freed the music of Scriabin's contemporary Sergei Rachmaninoff from all dross in his Lucerne retrospective and led it back to its melodic glowing core. Petrenko now achieves a similarly impressive vindication here.

The special and unique quality that festivals aim (and need) to offer should, of course, not merely extend to individual interpretive highlights, but ideally to entire evenings. So far this summer, there haven't been too many of them in Lucerne. Yannick Nézet-Séguin with the Metropolitan Opera New York Orchestra shows how it can be done.

It was the Met Orchestra's first guest performance at the KKL in 24 years. The performance was notable for its extraordinary level, but even more so for the warmth of its music-making, which lacked the cool precision fanaticism of other American orchestras. Instead, it was reminiscent of Leonard Bernstein's motto, «Let’s make music as friends,» which still shapes the spirit of the Lucerne Festival Orchestra today. No wonder Nézet-Séguin is one of the preferred guest conductors (and possible Chailly successors) there.

image.author: Manuela Jans / Lucerne Festival
image.caption: Charismatic, following in Bernstein's footsteps: Yannick Nézet-Séguin with vocalist Joyce DiDonato (right) and members of the Met Orchestra during the final applause at the KKL.

content.caption: Charismatic, following in Bernstein's footsteps: Yannick Nézet-Séguin with vocalist Joyce DiDonato (right) and members of the Met Orchestra during the final applause at the KKL.
content.author: Manuela Jans / Lucerne Festival

content.text: With his own people, he created a coherent program that explored the question of whether there wasn't something up there in the infinite expanses that gave meaning to all the earthly drama. The tone was set by American composer Missy Mazzoli with her «Sinfonia (for Orbiting Spheres),» which sounded appropriately unearthly thanks to the use of eight harmonicas. The destination was formed by Gustav Mahler's ambiguous vision of paradise in his 4th Symphony. On the way there, mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato traversed the shallows of the human sphere with her Rückert Lieder – including some audible problems in the high register.

But the almost symbiotic intimacy with which one thing flowed into another here quickly made this forgotten. Nézet-Séguin was a master at shaping every detail of the rich scores, without forgetting the much more important thing: to let the music breathe freely and organically. One had not heard the slow movement of the Fourth, in which time almost stood still, with such soul for a long time.

Who can come after that? Really, only one: Martha Argerich. The pianist of the century honored us on Monday with the Munich Philharmonic under Lahav Shani – and apparently was in a very bad mood at first. In any case, she plunges almost grimly into Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 2. She wants to know nothing of the alleged proximity of the piece to Mozart, playing alternately powerfully, then as if weightless, sometimes with pointed wit, sometimes with breathtaking brilliance. And one recognizes: no trace of a bad mood; it is simply the entire range of emotions that are so immediately reflected in Argerich's playing, grabbing and captivating one. For 85 years now, this has been unreservedly festival-worthy – it sweeps the people at the KKL from their seats.

Priska Ketterer /

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- The Lucerne Festival featured a compelling mix of conventional and innovative performances, including the Met Orchestra's first appearance in Lucerne in 24 years.
- Highlights included Martha Argerich's brilliant interpretation of Beethoven's 2nd Piano Concerto and a rarely performed symphony by Alexander Scriabin conducted by Kirill Petrenko.
- Yannick Nézet-Séguin impressed with an emotional program, standing out for his warm and intimate interpretations.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
- The Lucerne Festival showcased an exciting mix of conventional and innovative performances, including the Met Orchestra's first appearance in Lucerne in 24 years.
 Highlights included Martha Argerich's brilliant interpretation of Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 2 and a rarely performed symphony by Alexander Scriabin, conducted by Kirill Petrenko.
 - Yannick Nézet-Séguin impressed with an emotional program and stood out through his warm, heartfelt interpretation.
